Hs would be a bold man, or • simpleton, who would now-a-days base his political as- pirations in advocating parliamentary re- form as the one thing needful. Women's suffrage is toyed with rather than freely ad- vocated by the oldest reformers ; and the as- similation of the county franchise to that of the boroughs meets with a half-hearted sup- port. It was very different when the cry of Parliamentary Reform was raised half a cen- tury ago. It was then a passion with all politicians, in its advocacy by the Whigs and Liberal., in its opposition by the Tories. It became a 'est by whisk the popular princip- les of the Whigs, and of the Liberal party in general, were to be tried. With a House of Commons largely composed of members representing pocket boroughs, which meant nominlee of rich landlords, it WIN extremely probable that any minister who ventured to propse any 1110Ballre, favourable to religious liberty, or hostile to eorrupt expenditure, would be ti-rued out of office, and left in the cold—as was Lord Grey —till he became too old to take up the reigns of Government with pleasure. " There was no hope," says Earl :Emmen, " unleea Parliamentary Re- form were taken up and resolutely pursued, of arresting the course of political repression, religious intolerance, and wasteful expendi- ture, which wits upheld by all the strength of a great party, victorious in foreign war, fortified by the posseseione of boroughs, which gave • majority in the House of Com- mons, and apparently invincible from long poseeesion of Government patronage, spread- ing over the Church, the law, the army, the navy, and the colonies." The cry for reform was an old one. It naturally grew out of the abuees of the re- presentative system, and these waxed or waned with the ever changing conditione of the people. In the early periode there wan o fixed rule for the selection of the towns represented in the Lower House. Sir Francis Palpate in his charming little book "The Merchant mid the Friar," gives a pic- turesque account of a county election. The people were summoned to attend by the sae if, and in his preemieo they had to ehooee "Knights of the shire," who should render the King suit and service in Parlia- ment. The office was not an acceptable one, and many • ere the attempts at evasion, giving the worthy sheriff no little trouble. It was no light matter in those days to travel hundreds of miles on horseback, through districts infested with outlaws. But the King wanted his taithful Commons to support him in his contest+, with the la- parlous barons; above all he wanted them to fill hie enipty Exchequer. Hie writs were generally issued to the towns or districts that were most populous. But when the House of Commons became a great estate of the realm, it was felt that bounds must be I set to this arbitrary discretion. The privi- lege of the Crown fell into dieuse, and as it had not been handed over to the House of Commons to regulate itself, anomalies soon crept in; ol boroughs that had slowly de- cayed still sent their members, while new ones that increased rapidly in wealth and population remained unrepresented. Oliver Cromwell, with his oharaoteristio vigour, corrected this. He gave representa- tives to Manchester, Leeds, and Halifax; and ditifianchised a considerable number of decayed boroughs. He conferred the elec- tive franchise on every owner of land, what- ever the nature of his tenure might be. He also determined that Scotland and Ireland should send their members to the House of Commons. With the return of the Stewarts there was of course reaction, and the good work was undone; parliamentary reform lay dormant for nearly a cmtury. The glaring defects and vices of the repre- sentative system—the restricted and un- equal franchise, the bribery of small electoral bodies, and the corruption of the representa- tives themselves formed the strongest arguments for parliamentary reform. Tax movement bearing the above designa- tion has, by this time, we should say. over- come any latent prejudioe Or soepticism which may have attended its appearance in our midst. We way "prejudice' because it is notorious that many shortsighted, though excellent, persons sincerely think that Science is inimical to the higher interests of mankind; and we deem it unnecessary to adduce proof that this belief is irrational, and even absurd, seeing that such proof is abun- dantly accessible to any reader of history, and any experienced worker in the sacred cause of human progress. To fall back upon the notion that" Ignorance is the parent of Faith" must surely appear to all, except by a class blinded by the lowest self-interest, as • treachery to Truth, and a denial of "the Divinity that shapes our ends." Scep- ticism as to the power of Science to awaken an interest in the minds of our busy artisans and shopkeepers is also found amongst the professional and literary men of our provin- cial towns. And this feeling does not wholly lack justification. The workers in this field have to face much difficulty and disappoint- ment. They are rewarded with many kicks and few halfpence. But strong conviction, backed by patient and disinterested labour, ultimately carries the position, spite of op. position and indifference. The exigencies of our space do not permit of our reporting at length the lecture by Mr. Norman Lookyer which fittingly closed the splendid series for which we stand indebted to the Gilchrist Educational Trustees, but it is pleasant to note that Mr. T. O. Hylands elicited a very hearty recognition of the ser- vice rendered to the community by our towns- man—the Rev. H. W. Perris Referring to the former course, he reminded his audi- ence that the guarantee fund of £lOO had been absorbed by payment of the lecturers, and the thin attendance in the reserved seats, did not materially reduce the balance of ex- penditure over income. The course of lec- tures just concluded had barely covered the local expenses. How were future efforts to fare unless the people shelved a noble inde- pendence of foreign aid, took the matter so happily inaugurated into their own hands, and organised a committee to raise—say 400 subscriptions at five shillings each to put it on a sound buninese footing? We feel assured that this appeal did not hill on heedless ears, but that the thing is as good as done, and that the 800 who responded- so enthusiasti- cally will see to it that a movement so fruit- ful of good to our population is not checked by the want of necessary funds. As to the Lectures, and the eminent men who have delivered them, we might say much—but must needs refrain—such seed cannot fall wholly in vain, and the day will come when those who have poured forth out of the full treasury of their knowledge, facts, and thoughts of such mighty import, and those who have laboured to bring them face to face with the toiling thousands of their fellowmen, will rejoice together over a harvest of intellectual and moral acquisition of which only the first-fruits can now be seen, Many problems await solution in these days of change; there is not one which is not more or less implicat d in the program of science, and upon which physical re- search has not an important word to utter. He copilot but be a true friend to his neigh- bours, who raises their minds above the sordid cares of life, and sets them thinking about the universe, where absolute reason reigns. And if wonder be akin to worship I—as Thomas Carlyle has accustomed us to think—we may thus find that the rainbow of our delight, though distilled, as it were, from sensuous facts, flings, its consecrating radiance upon the mysterious heaven which overarches our earthly life.
